snapshot.title: Fundamental Rights Block 2: Art 19–22 (Right to Freedom)
snapshot.exam_hook: 🏔️ UPSC Ranker Hook: Art 19 suspended only in External Emergency. Art 20 & 21 NEVER suspended. Art 21 expanded by Maneka Gandhi case. Art 21A: 86th Amendment Art 22: Punitive vs Preventive.

quick_notes.title: Article 19: The Six Freedoms
quick_notes.detail: Art 19(1) guarantees 6 rights: Speech & Expression, Assembly (peaceful/no arms), Association (includes Co-operatives - 97th Amendment), Movement, Residence, and Profession. Restrictions : These are not absolute and can be restricted for sovereignty, integrity, security, public order, etc.
quick_notes.explanation: Article 19 of the Indian Constitution gives every citizen six basic freedoms, but these freedoms are not unlimited. The first freedom is the right to speak and express your opinions. The second is the right to gather peacefully without weapons. The third is the right to form groups or associations, which after the 97th Amendment in 2011 also includes the right to form cooperative societies. The fourth is the right to move freely anywhere in India, the fifth is the right to live in any part of the country, and the sixth is the right to practice any profession or carry on any occupation, trade, or business. However, the government can place reasonable restrictions on these freedoms for reasons like protecting India's sovereignty (supreme power or independence), integrity (unity), security, public order, decency, or morality.

quick_notes.title: Article 20: Protection in Conviction
quick_notes.detail: Three protections: 1. No Ex-post-facto Law (cannot be punished for an act that was not a crime when committed). 2. No Double Jeopardy (cannot be punished twice for same offence). 3. No Self-incrimination (cannot be forced to be a witness against oneself).
quick_notes.explanation: Article 20 of the Constitution of India gives you three specific protections if you are ever accused of a crime. First, it protects you from ex-post-facto law, which means you cannot be punished for an act that was not a crime at the time you did it; the law can only punish you for something that was already illegal when you committed the act. Second, it protects you from double jeopardy, which means you cannot be tried and punished more than once for the same offence, so if a court has already found you innocent or guilty, you cannot be put on trial again for that same crime. Third, it protects you from self-incrimination, which means you cannot be forced to be a witness against yourself, so no one can compel you to speak or give evidence that would prove you are guilty.

quick_notes.title: Article 21: Life and Personal Liberty
quick_notes.detail: "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to PROCEDURE ESTABLISHED BY LAW." SC in Maneka Gandhi case (1978) introduced "DUE PROCESS OF LAW" meaning the law itself must be just, fair, and reasonable.
quick_notes.explanation: Article 21 of the Indian Constitution says that no person can have their life taken away or their personal freedom taken away, except by following a procedure that is set by law. The Supreme Court, in the famous Maneka Gandhi case of 1978, changed the meaning of this article by introducing a new idea called "due process of law." "Due process of law" means that the law which takes away your life or freedom must not just be any law, but it must be a law that is itself just, fair, and reasonable. So even if a law exists, if it is unfair or unreasonable, it cannot be used to take away your life or personal liberty. This makes Article 21 a very strong protection for every person's right to live and to be free.

quick_notes.title: Article 21A: Right to Education
quick_notes.detail: Added by 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002. State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of 6 to 14 years. It made education a Fundamental Right.
quick_notes.explanation: Article 21A is a part of the Indian Constitution that was added by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act in the year 2002. This Article says that the State, meaning the government, must provide free and compulsory education to every child between the ages of 6 and 14 years. Free education means no child has to pay any fees for schooling, and compulsory education means it is the duty of the government and parents to ensure the child attends school. Before this amendment, education was only a Directive Principle, which was not enforceable in court, but Article 21A made it a Fundamental Right, which means a citizen can go to court if the government does not provide this education. A Fundamental Right is a basic right guaranteed by the Constitution that the government cannot take away and that courts can enforce. So, Article 21A guarantees that every Indian child aged 6 to 14 has the legal right to free and compulsory education.

quick_notes.title: Article 22: Arrest and Detention
quick_notes.detail: Two types: 1. Punitive (after trial). 2. Preventive (before trial/to prevent crime). Rights under Punitive : informed of grounds, right to consult lawyer, produced before magistrate in 24 hours. Preventive detention can be for 3 months (can be extended by Advisory Board).
quick_notes.explanation: Article 22 of the Indian Constitution deals with arrest and detention. There are two types: punitive detention, which happens after a trial and conviction for a crime, and preventive detention, where a person is locked up before any trial to stop them from possibly committing a crime. For punitive detention, the arrested person has three rights: to be told the reasons for arrest, to consult and be defended by a lawyer, and to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours. For preventive detention, a person can be held for up to three months without trial; if the government wants to detain them longer, an Advisory Board made up of High Court judges must approve the extension. These protections apply to all individuals, not just citizens.

topic_title: Fundamental Rights Block 2: Art 19–22 (Right to Freedom)
lesson_intro: The 'Right to Freedom' is the backbone of individual liberty in the Indian Constitution. Article 19 alone provides six fundamental freedoms that allow us to live as free citizens in a democracy. However, these freedoms are not absolute; they come with 'reasonable restrictions'. This block also contains the most expanded article in constitutional history—Article 21 (Protection of Life and Personal Liberty). Through judicial activism, Art 21 has grown to include the right to privacy, clean environment, and even the right to sleep. Understanding this block is crucial for both Prelims (direct articles) and Mains (liberty vs. security debates).
